paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Across the dry belt that stretches from North Africa through Iran to Central Asia and western China, travellers often notice lines of small mounds running across the plain, each with a hole at its centre. From the air they look like rows of craters. They are in fact the surface traces of one of the oldest water technologies still in use: the qanat, an underground channel that carries groundwater by gravity from the foot of the hills to fields and villages, sometimes many kilometres away. The technique is known by different names in different regions: karez in Afghanistan and western China, foggara in Algeria and falaj in Oman. The basic principle, however, is the same everywhere.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Building a qanat begins with a search for water. A skilled digger, traditionally called a muqanni in Iran, studies the slope of an alluvial fan, the wedge of gravel and sand that streams deposit where they leave the mountains, looking for signs of moisture such as patches of vegetation. He then sinks a trial well, known as the mother well, until it reaches the water table. If the flow is reliable, the real work can start. Rather than working downwards from the mother well, the diggers usually begin at the far end, where the channel will come to the surface, and tunnel back uphill towards the source.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The tunnel itself has a very gentle gradient. If it falls too steeply, the fast-moving water erodes the walls and the channel can collapse; if it is too flat, the water barely moves and silt builds up. At regular intervals along the route a vertical shaft is dug from the surface down to the tunnel. These shafts, which create the familiar lines of mounds, let the workers remove excavated soil, bring in fresh air and keep their direction underground. Once the qanat is finished, the same shafts provide access for cleaning and repair, work that has to be done regularly if the channel is to keep flowing.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The great advantage of the system is that the water travels out of sight. In a climate where summer temperatures are high and the air is very dry, an open canal can lose a large share of its water to evaporation before it reaches the fields. Underground, the losses are much smaller. A qanat also needs no pump and no fuel: as long as the aquifer is recharged by rain and snowmelt in the mountains, water arrives day and night without any outside energy. And because the channel only collects water that flows into it naturally, a qanat cannot easily take more from the aquifer than the aquifer receives.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Qanats shaped not only farming but also the way communities were organised. Since a single channel might serve dozens of families, there had to be rules about who received water and for how long. In many villages the flow was divided by time, with each household entitled to a fixed share of hours in a cycle that repeated every week or two. Some desert towns also used the cool, steady flow for purposes beyond irrigation. In parts of Iran, qanat water helped to cool houses in the hot months, and in winter it was used to make ice, which was then kept in large domed buildings and used through the summer.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Today many qanats are in decline. Modern motor-driven wells can draw water from much deeper levels, and when they lower the water table, the older channels above them simply run dry. Many young people have also moved to the cities, and fewer are willing to do the hard and sometimes dangerous work of maintenance. Yet interest in the technology is growing again. In 2016 a group of Iranian qanats was added to UNESCO's World Heritage List, and engineers concerned about climate change have begun to study qanats as an example of how a water supply can be managed within the limits of what nature provides.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Concrete is the most widely used construction material on Earth. It is cheap, it can be poured into almost any shape, and it is enormously strong when squeezed. Its weakness is tension. When concrete is stretched or bent, it cracks easily, which is why most structural concrete contains steel reinforcing bars that carry the tensile loads. Yet even well-reinforced concrete develops fine cracks over time, as it shrinks while drying, expands and contracts with changes in temperature, and carries the loads of traffic and wind.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: A small crack is rarely dangerous in itself. The problem is what it lets in. Water, carrying dissolved salts from the sea or from the chemicals spread on winter roads to melt ice, can travel through cracks to the steel inside. There it causes rust, and because rust takes up more space than the original metal, it pushes the surrounding concrete apart, widening the crack and letting in still more water. Left unchecked, this cycle can weaken a bridge or a car park long before the end of its planned life. Inspecting and repairing cracks is therefore one of the largest costs of looking after concrete structures.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Engineers have long known that concrete has a limited ability to repair itself. Some of the cement in a mix never fully reacts with water during construction. When a fine crack later lets moisture in, these leftover particles can react, and the products, together with calcium carbonate that forms when the concrete reacts with carbon dioxide from the air, may gradually block the gap. This natural process, called autogenous healing, works only for very narrow cracks, however, and it is too slow and unpredictable to be relied on when a structure is designed.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: One of the best-known attempts to improve on it began at Delft University of Technology in the Netherlands, where the microbiologist Henk Jonkers and his colleagues asked whether bacteria could do the job. The challenge was to find organisms that could survive inside concrete, which is highly alkaline and becomes as hard as rock. The team chose bacteria that form spores: tough, dormant cells that can stay alive for long periods without food or water. The spores are mixed into the concrete together with a food source, such as calcium lactate, and remain inactive for as long as the material is undamaged.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: When a crack forms and water enters, the spores become active. The bacteria feed on the calcium lactate and, as a by-product, produce calcium carbonate, essentially limestone, which gradually fills the crack and seals it against further water. Because the bacteria also consume oxygen, their activity also reduces the oxygen available to the steel, giving it additional protection against rust. Once the crack is closed, conditions inside become hostile again and the surviving bacteria return to a dormant state, ready to respond if new damage occurs.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Bacterial concrete is not the only approach being explored. Some researchers add tiny capsules filled with a healing agent, which break open when a crack passes through them and release a liquid that hardens in the gap. Others have looked to the past. Many concrete structures built by the ancient Romans are still standing after two thousand years, and a study published in 2023 by a team including researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology suggested one reason: small lumps of lime in Roman concrete, long dismissed as a sign of careless mixing, appear to act as a store of calcium that can react with water and fill cracks.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Despite these advances, self-healing concrete remains a specialist product. It costs more to produce than ordinary concrete, and the healing agents can affect the strength of the mix if they are not added carefully. Its supporters argue that the price should be judged over the whole life of a structure rather than at the moment of construction: if a self-healing material avoids even a few rounds of inspection and repair, it may turn out to be the cheaper choice. There is an environmental argument too. Making cement releases large amounts of carbon dioxide, so any material that allows structures to last longer, and to be replaced less often, could help to reduce the industry's impact on the climate.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the 1880s the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus carried out a long series of experiments on the only subject who was always available to him: himself. To study memory without the influence of meaning, he made up lists of nonsense syllables, short combinations of letters that formed no real word, memorised them, and then measured how much time he needed to learn each list again after delays of hours or days. He found that forgetting was fastest soon after learning and then slowed down, a pattern now known as the forgetting curve. He also noticed something of even greater practical value: lists that he had studied in several sessions spread out over time were retained far better than lists he had learned in a single sitting.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: This finding, the spacing effect, has since been confirmed in a very large number of studies, with learners of all ages and with many kinds of material, from vocabulary and historical facts to mathematical procedures and physical skills. The basic result is remarkably consistent. If the total amount of study time is kept the same, dividing it into separate sessions with gaps between them produces better long-term memory than concentrating it into one block. Massed practice, as cramming is called by researchers, can be effective for a test the next morning, but much of what is learned in this way is lost within days.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why should a gap help? One explanation is that, when material is reviewed immediately, it is still fresh in the mind, so the review requires little effort and adds little to memory. After a delay, some of the material has begun to fade, and recalling it takes work. The psychologist Robert Bjork has described such obstacles as desirable difficulties: conditions that make learning feel slower and harder at the time but lead to stronger and longer-lasting memories. The same idea helps to explain a related finding known as the testing effect. Students who try to recall information from memory, for example by answering questions, typically remember it better a week later than students who spend the same time simply rereading it, even though rereading often feels more productive.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Turning these findings into a daily routine is not straightforward, because the best interval between reviews depends on how well something is already known. In the early 1970s the German journalist Sebastian Leitner proposed a simple solution that needed nothing more than a box with several compartments and a set of flashcards. Every new card starts in the first compartment, which is reviewed most often. When a learner answers a card correctly, it moves to the next compartment, which is reviewed less frequently; when the answer is wrong, the card goes back to the first compartment, however far it had progressed. Difficult items therefore come up again and again, while well-known ones appear only occasionally, so that study time is concentrated where it is most needed.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: From the late 1980s onwards, computer programs automated the same logic, estimating for each item the moment at which it is likely to be forgotten and scheduling a review shortly before then. Such software is now widely used by language learners and by medical students, who must memorise very large numbers of facts. The programs differ in their details, but they share Leitner's central insight that the interval between reviews should grow as an item becomes better known.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Despite the strength of the evidence, spaced practice is far less common than it could be. Part of the reason lies in how learning feels. Cramming produces a quick sense of mastery: after an evening of repetition, the material seems familiar, and familiarity is easily mistaken for knowledge. Spacing, by contrast, means meeting material that has partly slipped away, which can be discouraging. School timetables add a further obstacle, since topics are often taught in a single block and then left behind once the end-of-unit test is over. Researchers who study learning argue that the answer is not more hours of study but a different arrangement of the same hours, with earlier topics returned to again and again throughout a course.
